questions.stem: A patient with known Addison's disease is admitted in Addisonian (adrenal) crisis with BP 68/40, confusion, and vomiting following a viral illness. Which initial interventions are CORRECT? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus immediately
Initiate 0.9% normal saline 1 L IV bolus for hemodynamic support
Administer fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally for mineralocorticoid replacement
Hold corticosteroids until ACTH stimulation test confirms adrenal insufficiency

questions.rationale: Addisonian crisis is life-threatening and requires: (1) immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (glucocorticoid replacement — the priority), and (2) aggressive NS fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia and hyponatremia (B). Fludrocortisone (C) is used for chronic mineralocorticoid replacement but is not the initial treatment in a crisis — hydrocortisone at high doses provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. Withholding steroids to do testing (D) is dangerous — diagnosis is clinical in a crisis. ACTH stimulation can be done later.

"Administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus immediately" fits the safer response to the cue "A patient with known Addison's disease is admitted in Addisonian (adrenal) crisis with BP 68/40, confusion".

The stem cue "Addisonian crisis is life-threatening and requires: (1) immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV (glucocorticoid replacement — the priority)" makes medication toxicity the active safety concern.
distractorRationales.d: The safer response addresses medication toxicity; "Hold corticosteroids until ACTH stimulation test confirms adrenal insufficiency" moves care toward routine care before medication-safety intervention.

questions.takeaway: Addisonian crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + NS bolus immediately. Do not delay for confirmatory testing.

questions.stem: A patient delivers vaginally and 30 minutes later has an estimated blood loss of 750 mL with a soft, boggy uterus displaced to the right. BP is 94/58, HR 118. Which sequence of interventions is correct?

options.text: IV oxytocin infusion, bimanual uterine compression, empty the bladder, call the provider
Empty the bladder, fundal massage, IV oxytocin infusion, call the provider if no improvement
Call the provider, obtain type and crossmatch, begin blood transfusion
Place in Trendelenburg, administer IV epinephrine, call for hysterectomy consent

questions.rationale: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) from uterine atony management: (1) Massage the fundus — stimulates uterine contraction. (2) Empty the bladder — a full bladder displaces the uterus and prevents contraction (uterus displaced to the right = full bladder). (3) IV oxytocin — first-line uterotonic. (4) Notify provider if no response. Bladder emptying is critical and often overlooked — the displaced, boggy uterus signals bladder distension. Epinephrine (D) and hysterectomy are not indicated at this stage.
questions.takeaway: Boggy uterus displaced to the right after delivery = full bladder; empty bladder first, then fundal massage + oxytocin.

questions.stem: A patient on clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia develops fever 39.8°C, diaphoresis, severe muscle rigidity ('lead pipe'), altered mental status, and autonomic instability (fluctuating BP, tachycardia). Which condition is this, and what is the immediate action?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome; administer cyproheptadine and stop all serotonergic agents
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS); discontinue antipsychotic immediately and initiate supportive care with dantrolene or bromocriptine
Acute dystonia; administer IV diphenhydramine 50 mg
Anticholinergic toxicity from clozapine; administer physostigmine

questions.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotics characterized by the tetrad: hyperthermia, severe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. It develops over days-weeks. Immediate management: stop the antipsychotic, aggressive cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene (muscle relaxant) and/or bromocriptine (dopamine agonist). Serotonin syndrome (A) has similar features but presents with hyperreflexia and clonus (not lead-pipe rigidity) and requires cyproheptadine. Acute dystonia (C) does not include fever or autonomic instability.

Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.d: The option can leave medication toxicity untreated because it commits to a competing cause before checking the dangerous pattern. questions.stem: An RN delegates to an LPN/LVN. Which task is within the LPN's scope of practice in most states?

options.text: Perform the initial nursing admission assessment for a newly admitted patient
Administer oral, IM, and subcutaneous medications and monitor response
Develop and update the nursing care plan based on patient assessment findings
Interpret cardiac rhythm strips and adjust IV vasopressor infusions per protocol

questions.rationale: LPN/LVN scope of practice typically includes: administering medications (oral, IM, SC, topical), performing basic wound care, collecting specimens, and monitoring and reporting patient status. Initial assessments (A) require RN-level nursing judgment and are an RN responsibility. Care plan development (C) is an RN function. Interpreting arrhythmias and adjusting vasopressors (D) requires advanced critical care RN knowledge. questions.stem: A 24-year-old on haloperidol develops sudden onset torticollis (involuntary neck twisting), oculogyric crisis (eyes fixed upward), and severe muscle rigidity within 3 days of starting the medication. Which type of extrapyramidal symptom (EPS) is this, and what is the antidote?

options.text: Tardive dyskinesia; no effective antidote, may require medication discontinuation
Akathisia; treat with propranolol or benzodiazepines
Acute dystonia; treat with IV/IM diphenhydramine or benztropine
Pseudoparkinsonism; treat with amantadine or reduce antipsychotic dose

questions.rationale: Acute dystonia presents within hours to days of starting a high-potency antipsychotic (like haloperidol) as sudden, painful muscle spasms — torticollis, oculogyric crisis, opisthotonus. Treatment is IV or IM diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or benztropine (Cogentin), which are anticholinergic agents. Tardive dyskinesia (A) develops after months-years of use as involuntary repetitive movements (lip smacking, tongue protrusion). Akathisia (B) is inner restlessness and urge to move. Pseudoparkinsonism (D) mimics Parkinson's disease with tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia.

distractorRationales.a: The cue "Pseudoparkinsonism (D) mimics Parkinson's disease with tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia" suggests medication toxicity, so "Tardive dyskinesia; no effective antidote, may require medication discontinuation" would not correct the active problem. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.b: "Akathisia; treat with propranolol or benzodiazepines" moves to activity, intake, or discharge planning too early. The cue "A 24-year-old on haloperidol develops sudden onset torticollis (involuntary neck twisting), oculogyric crisis (eyes fixed upward)" raises concern for medication toxicity, so medication-safety intervention is needed before ambulation, intake, or discharge teaching.
distractorRationales.d: "Pseudoparkinsonism; treat with amantadine or reduce antipsychotic dose" misses the bedside risk. The cue "A 24-year-old on haloperidol develops sudden onset torticollis (involuntary neck twisting), oculogyric crisis (eyes fixed upward)" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.

questions.takeaway: Acute dystonia (torticollis, oculogyric crisis) within days of antipsychotic = IV/IM diphenhydramine or benztropine (anticholinergics).

questions.stem: After fundal massage and oxytocin, a postpartum patient's uterus remains atonic and bleeding continues. The provider orders methylergonovine (Methergine) 0.2 mg IM. Which patient condition is an absolute contraindication to this medication?

options.text: History of asthma
Hypertension with BP currently 158/100 mmHg
Breastfeeding
Gestational diabetes

questions.rationale: Methylergonovine (Methergine) is an ergot alkaloid uterotonic that causes powerful vasoconstriction. It is absolutely contraindicated in hypertension (including pre-eclampsia) because it can cause severe hypertensive crisis, stroke, and coronary artery spasm. Asthma (A) is a relative contraindication for prostaglandins (like carboprost/Hemabate) but not for Methergine. Breastfeeding (C) is not a contraindication — it is safe during breastfeeding. Gestational diabetes (D) is not a contraindication.

questions.stem: A patient with a known adrenal mass is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma. The pre-operative medication orders include phenoxybenzamine (alpha-blocker). The surgeon also wants to start a beta-blocker. The nurse understands that the CORRECT order for pre-operative blockade is:

options.text: Beta-blocker first, then alpha-blocker after adequate heart rate control
Alpha-blocker first for 7–14 days, then beta-blocker added if needed
Both alpha and beta-blockers started simultaneously on day 1
Beta-blocker alone is sufficient; alpha-blockers are unnecessary pre-operatively

questions.rationale: Alpha-blockade MUST be established before beta-blockade in pheochromocytoma. Pheos release primarily epinephrine and norepinephrine, causing vasoconstriction via alpha receptors. If a beta-blocker is given first, it blocks the vasodilatory beta-2 effect without blocking alpha-mediated vasoconstriction — resulting in paradoxical, unopposed hypertensive crisis. Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) is initiated 7–14 days pre-op; beta-blocker is added only after alpha-blockade is established, if needed for tachycardia.

distractorRationales.a: The safer response addresses medication toxicity; "Beta-blocker first, then alpha-blocker after adequate heart rate control" moves care toward routine care before medication-safety intervention.
distractorRationales.c: The cue "A patient with a known adrenal mass is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma" suggests medication toxicity, so "Both alpha and beta-blockers started simultaneously on day 1" would not correct the active problem. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.d: This distractor shifts care toward misprioritization instead of medication-safety intervention. The stem cue "The pre-operative medication orders include phenoxybenzamine (alpha-blocker)" makes medication toxicity the active safety concern.

questions.takeaway: Pheochromocytoma pre-op: alpha-block FIRST (7–14 days), then add beta-blocker. Never beta-block first — causes unopposed hypertensive crisis.

questions.stem: A client 12 hours after transsphenoidal hypophysectomy has a steady drip of clear drainage from the nose and reports a salty taste in the throat. Which action should the nurse take first?

questions.stem: A patient reports chest pressure and becomes hypotensive and tachycardic. What is the most useful bedside interpretation?

options.text: The patient may be having an acute cardiovascular emergency
The pain is likely harmless because the patient is still awake
The heart rate change is the only issue
The blood pressure will likely fix itself without reassessment

questions.rationale: Chest pressure with hypotension and tachycardia is concerning for an unstable cardiac event and requires immediate reassessment. **Why the others are wrong:** - B Awake status does not make the chest pain safe. - C The whole pattern matters, not just the heart rate. - D Waiting for spontaneous correction is unsafe.

questions.stem: A toddler has had vomiting and diarrhea for two days. Which finding should the nurse recognize as most concerning for dehydration?

options.text: Fewer wet diapers than usual

Mild irritability at nap time
A normal appetite earlier in the week
